lesson.title: The Promise That Sealed Ratification
lesson.summary: The Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments to the Constitution ratified in December 1791, fulfilled the promise Federalists had made to Anti-Federalist critics that individual liberties would be explicitly protected once the new government took effect.
lesson.body:
The absence of a bill of rights had been one of the Anti-Federalists' loudest objections during the ratification debates, and it was not an objection Federalists could simply dismiss. In several closely divided states, Federalist supporters of the Constitution secured ratification only by promising that a bill of rights would be added as amendments once the new government was up and running, an arrangement historians sometimes call the Massachusetts Compromise after the state where the pattern first took clear shape in 1788.

James Madison, ironically, had originally argued against including a bill of rights at all, reasoning in Federalist No. 84 that since the national government only held the specific powers listed in the Constitution, it had no power to violate rights that were never granted to it in the first place, and that listing certain rights might dangerously imply that any rights left off the list were unprotected. But Madison also understood practical politics, and once elected to the first House of Representatives, he took on the task of drafting amendments himself, partly to make good on Federalist promises and partly to head off Anti-Federalist calls for a potentially far more disruptive second constitutional convention.

Madison drew heavily on existing state declarations of rights, particularly George Mason's 1776 Virginia Declaration of Rights, as he worked through dozens of proposed amendments submitted by state ratifying conventions and narrowed them down to a workable list. Congress approved twelve amendments in September 1789 and sent them to the states; ten were ratified and took effect on December 15, 1791, becoming the Bill of Rights.

The amendments protected a wide range of individual liberties that the original Constitution had left unstated. The First Amendment protected freedom of speech, religion, the press, and assembly. The Second addressed the right to bear arms. The Fourth protected against unreasonable searches and seizures, while the Fifth guaranteed due process and protection against self-incrimination, and the Sixth guaranteed the right to a speedy trial. The Eighth barred cruel and unusual punishment. The Tenth Amendment, closely tied to the federalism the Constitution had established, reaffirmed that any powers not delegated to the national government were reserved to the states or to the people.

By adding these protections, the framers addressed the core Anti-Federalist fear that a stronger national government, of the kind the Constitutional Convention had created, might otherwise trample the individual liberties Americans had fought a revolution to secure. The Bill of Rights did not resolve every tension built into the new government, but it closed the ratification debate and gave the Constitution the broad legitimacy it needed as George Washington's new administration began governing under it.
